utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Mr. Registrar, can you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is case IT-95-14/1, the Prosecutor versus Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Can we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Meddegoda, Ms. Sutherland and Ms. Erasmus for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The Defence, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Goran Mikulicic representing the Defence, alongside with Mr. Joka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So, we shall continue with the testimony of yesterday's witness. Can you pull down the blinds, please? Thank you very much. (The witness entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, Sir. Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Have you slept well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We are going to continue to hear your testimony. I wish to remind you that you took a solemn oath yesterday to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Are you still bound by that statement today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You are going to answer questions put to you by Defence counsel, that is, Mr. Mikulicic, this morning. Mr. Mikulicic, your witness. WITNESS S (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Mr. S, my name is Goran Mikulicic. I am an attorney from Zagreb and, in this case, I represent the Defence. After answering questions by my learned colleague the Prosecutor yesterday, it is my turn today, and I should like to ask you kindly to answer them to the best of your recollection. Mr. S, in your testimony yesterday you said that you were used on two occasions as a human shield; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. S, please, according to your understanding, what is a "human shield" and what is the purpose of a "human shield"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my understanding, I was a human shield by being exposed to somebody who is firing in a certain direction and I am exposed to the fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that, according to your understanding, to be exposed to fire as a human shield assumes a movement towards a certain target in the aim of the protection of men behind that "human shield"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The people behind me are protected, the aim being for those in front of us not to fire and to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well, you have now explained your understanding of a "human shield". If my memory does not fail me, I think you said that you were used, together with other people, as a human shield first near the village of Skradno; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could I ask for the usher's assistance, to place on the ELMO the photograph which has been admitted into evidence as Prosecution Exhibit 102? (Handed). I think it is alright now, thank you. Mr. S, let us just remind ourselves; will you tell us, please, what these markings that you put on the photograph represent, starting from the letter "A". What is the letter "A", please -- please speak into the microphone so we can hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the Kaonik camp; "B" the place we were used as a human shield towards Skradno; "C" is the place where we got off the bus when we started towards the village of Strane; "D" is the extreme point we reached as a human shield in the direction of Strane; and "E" is the direction from which, as I understood it, the bullets were being fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us go back for a moment to the part of the photograph that you marked with the letter "B" in the upper right-hand corner. It is the place where you were lined up as a human shield. Can you tell us, regarding this point that you have marked with "B", where is the village of Skradno?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The village of Skradno cannot be seen on this photograph well -- the first houses are Croat houses, these houses (indicating) and then behind them is the village of Skradno, going uphill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How far is the village of Skradno behind these first Croat houses in relation to the position where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The beginning may be about 300 or 400 metres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you saw those first houses of the village of Skradno -- I am talking about the Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you see the villagers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether, in the village of Skradno, there were any BiH army units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said, if my memory is correct, that one man went to the village of Skradno to negotiate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry, maybe I misunderstood then. Do you know whether a man from your group went to the village of Skradno to negotiate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say that he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I am asking you whether you know that he did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: My next question then is whether anyone from your group did go to Skradno for negotiations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the results of those negotiations were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The surrender of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was there any fire exchanged during this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not hear any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you and the people who were at spot "B" move at all from that spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The position that I have marked as the final position is the position that we held for maybe 10 or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And, after that, you withdrew and got into the buses, if I remember well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that, you headed towards position "C"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Position "C" is the position where you got off the bus; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After that, you went on foot along this road that you marked with an arrow; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How many metres did you cover on foot, roughly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After about 50 metres, we reached this position (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This cross-roads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a position that cannot be seen from above.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Seen from where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people in Strane cannot see this position -- there is a little hill here protecting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And then you reached point "D"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How far is position "D" from this intersection where you have marked a second arrow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 70 to 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. S, from this position that you marked with the letter "D", viewing it from that direction, where is the village of Strane?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The village of Strane -- again, it cannot be seen on this photograph, but it is up here in this direction (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you perhaps find your way on a photograph that would show the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In that case, I would like to ask the usher for his assistance to put under the ELMO a photograph showing a larger area, for instance, exhibit number 95. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. S, can you find your way on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you show us with the pointer where the village of Strane is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness indicates on map).

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your view, how far is the village of Strane from the position where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, about 200, 300, maybe 400 metres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you see any villagers in the village of Strane?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I saw no-one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the BiH army was in the village of Strane?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you describe to us what happened when you stopped on the road on the position that you marked with the letter "D" -- what happened then? Sorry for interrupting you -- another question before that -- how many HVO soldiers were with your group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 15 or 20.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the population of the village of Strane is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Not even roughly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe 100 or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How many households does it have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 50, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you said that there were about 15 HVO soldiers with your group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At least 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what is the most -- at most?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know -- I did not dare count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. S, is it true that you said that, when you reached the village of Strane, HVO soldiers went in front and surrounded the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not go in front, but they went to the side, that is, to the left (indicates). We saw them here (indicates) from this road we could see them coming out of this wood (indicates) and spreading out towards the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How many soldiers stayed behind with you, if those others went towards the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not the same soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, they were other soldiers. I see, I did not get that. Mr. S, tell us, did you and your colleagues who were on the road at that time -- did you move towards the village of Strane, or did you stand where you were as you did in the other case, in the case of the Skradno village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From this bend in the road we started moving (indicates) and we moved slowly forward, the HVO soldiers went behind us and they fired. At that time these soldiers, too, were moving towards the village (indicates), so that that was the final point that we reached and it ended there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Which is that final point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the point I marked with the letter "D", 10 or 15 metres in front of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us where you were -- is there a visual connection -- can you see the village from the position where you were? Can you see the houses in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the first houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And those further away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because the village is in a slope. From this position (indicates) you can see the first houses, the beginning of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us what happened then? Did that village surrender, or was there any fighting around the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The village surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you see a white flag or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not -- I saw nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In this case, too, did someone go to negotiate from your group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him coming back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was that the same man who went to negotiate at the village of Skradno?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see anyone going at the village of Skradno, but I know that somebody did, and in this second case I did see somebody coming back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How much time went by from when he went and when he came back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had gone before we got there, so I did not see him going, I only saw him coming back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us how much time went by while you were standing there from the moment he came back? Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You got there, you stopped on the road in front of the bridge and you spent some time there. How much time did it take for the man to come back while you were standing there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you, because I do not know when he went.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I did not ask you when he went, I asked you when he came back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we reached that point we might have gone on if he had not come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That is what I am asking you. How long did you stand there before he came back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came down hill -- you cannot see the path well (indicates) and, when he got somewhere here (indicates) -- you cannot see him because of the trees or shrubs, and we saw him and at that moment a car came to pick him up and took him off somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. S, you said that, at that point in time, you heard fire. Can you tell us where the shooting was coming from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, it was coming from somewhere here (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How can you tell that? Did you see the shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but it was -- the shots were whizzing by and sometimes we would bend down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was anyone wounded among you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no-one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will not need the photograph anymore, Mr. Usher. Mr. S, during your stay in Kaonik, did you ask to be taken to a doctor ever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not ask for a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. S, do you know whether some other prisoners asked to be taken to a doctor and whether they were taken to see a doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think -- yes, I know of one case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. S, after you were released on 8 February, I think, from Kaonik, did you stay in those parts, or did you leave those parts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And, since then, you have not been back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to my place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am thinking of the place where you lived before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have the same place in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours, the Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Witness S, the Chamber has no further questions for you. Therefore, you have completed your testimony here. We wish to thank you for coming, and we wish you a happy journey to your country. Thank you very much. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The next witness appears as the 11th witness on our list in paragraph 4 of our motion filed on 20 March 1998. Your Honours, this witness is not of Bosnian or Bosniak ethnicity, but in fact is Syrian. He is Islamic, but because of his ethnicity, and the circumstances that happened during the course of the war with people such as himself, he seeks protective measures and he is still residing in Bosnia, so, your Honours, we have written to Mr. Mikulicic about this witness and informed him that we would be seeking to make this application today. We seek, your Honour, that he be given a pseudonym, Witness T, and that the image of his face be distorted in such a way that he cannot be recognised. That is our application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect, for the protection of the witness which was presented up to now by our learned colleague, the Prosecutor, you know all too well that we never objected to protective measures for Bosniak citizens. But, we have heard here from the Prosecutor that the person in question is not a Bosnian citizen. It is a person of quite different nationality and that is why the Defence cannot see why protective measures should apply for this witness. Therefore, in this particular case, the Defence objects to protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you, but Mr. Niemann told us that this person lives in Bosnia still.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. The witness will explain that in the course of his evidence. In fact, he lived in Bosnia for a period I think of 15 years, prior to the war. But he is of course not Bosniak -- he is Syrian, but, in our submission, it is a distinction without a difference and your Honours have heard evidence of the treatment of people who were classified as mudjehadeen in the camp and they were certainly singled out and treated differently, which, in our submission, would give rise to very genuine fears. So this witness has been there for a considerable period of time and merely to discriminate against him on the basis that he may not have citizenship -- he certainly has residency and has had it for 15 years -- in our submission, your Honours that would be unfair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, excuse me that I have interrupted you. You can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Taking into account the position of the Prosecution, the Defence nevertheless maintains its position. We think there is no reason to apply protective measures for foreign citizens in view of the events that took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: If I understood you well, Mr. Niemann, it is a person who is not of -- who is not Bosnian -- it is a Syrian-born person who has been living for the past 15 years in Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I will consult my colleagues now. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me, please. The Trial Chamber will grant protective measures asked for by the Prosecution, because the Trial Chamber does not think it should differentiate in this case between the Syrian born person and the other witnesses, so, in the same way this Trial Chamber has granted protective measures for other witnesses, this Trial Chamber is going to grant protective measures requested for this particular witness. We are going to take all necessary steps now, in order to be able to carry out these measures. In which case, could the witness be brought in? (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, Sir. Can you hear me? So, this is the witness and you, madam, are the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes. (Interpreter at the witness stand).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: According to Article 76 of our Rules, each interpreter or translator has to make the oath that they will perform their task with commitment and impartiality and in full respect of confidentiality. So, I am addressing myself, to you, the interpreter. Are you prepared to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, I agree to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I will now address myself to the witness. The witness has now to read a solemn declaration and the usher has to give him this declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, may God be my witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You may be seated and you can now answer the questions which Mr. Niemann, the Prosecutor, is going to ask you, taking into account, obviously, that you should speak rather slowly and stop so that we can use four languages in this courtroom. Mr. Niemann, the floor is yours? WITNESS T

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness, their Honours have granted to you certain protective measures in that the image of your face will be distorted so that it cannot be recognised and, during the course of your testimony, we will refer to you by a pseudonym, Witness T. So, when you are giving your testimony, you should not use your name, but I would ask you to look at the piece of paper that I am now going to show you and I would ask you to tell us whether or not your name is written on that paper. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, if your Honours please. Might it be marked Prosecution exhibit number in order, and tendered under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 103.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness, what is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Syrian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what is your religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How old are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in 1962, 35 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What languages do you speak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I speak Arabic, Serbo-Croat, and a little bit of French.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is Arabic your native tongue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Arabic is my mother-tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, before the war in Yugoslavia, the former Yugoslavia, in 1992-93, for how long had you lived in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I started living in Bosnia in 1982.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, when you lived in Bosnia, did you undertake studies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And for how long did you study medicine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stopped at third year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And since the war, have you become married?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I was released from prison, I married.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And your wife, where was she born, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My wife is Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Prior to the war, what work did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not engaged in any form of employment -- I was a student -- I went to medical school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When the war broke out in 1992, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent 20 days in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, after that, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, I decided to return to Bosnia to stand by the Bosnian people, to do what ever I can for the Bosnian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I returned from Zagreb to Travnik. Upon arriving there, I joined the military units attached to the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what was your position -- what role did you play in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I served for seven days and I worked as a nurse -- a male nurse. I helped with first-aid and all ancillary medical work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After your seven days' service, what did you then do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the seventh day, I found it difficult to cope with the situation -- I could not face war -- and decided to get involved in relief work as an interpreter and started teaching youth the Arabic language, and religious education -- Islamic religious education.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As an interpreter, who did you interpret for -- in what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To start with, I worked -- I started self-employed and I had my students and I worked with various bodies, including an Egyptian body, as an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why was there a necessity to have an Egyptian or Arabic interpreter in Bosnia at this time -- why did they need such interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Relief agencies operating in the area needed somebody who could use the local language and there was a great demand for interpreters. That is where I came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By relief agencies, are you talking about humanitarian agencies from the Arabic countries; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, there were Arab relief agencies in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I want to move on to 1993, if I may. About 25 May 1993, what happened to you -- what did you decide to do -- what were you doing on that day in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I decided to go back to Syria and there was a relief convoy -- trucks -- and I had this will in me to travel on this convoy, against the advice of other people. On that convoy was a Croat person who had an estate Lada and a friend of mine, in Travnik, advised me to make the trip with him, in his car, so that will be useful to get past checkpoints. I accepted the advice of this friend and I took the car of this Croat person. What happened is that we started the trip ahead of the convoy in an area three or four kilometres outside Travnik -- the area called Kocava and we were supposed to wait for the trucks at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This convoy was the United Nations convoy, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my knowledge, yes, it was an UN convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: While you were awaiting for the UN convoy to reach you, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We arrived at the Croat checkpoint, the driver pulled in, and a Croat soldier approached us and asked for papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did you know he was a Croat soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the badge and the emblem on his outfit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened when the Croat soldier approached you -- what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He took the papers. There was the Croat driver and a Croat passenger and I was in the back seat. When he asked for their papers, he collected the papers from them and he asked for identification from me, so I gave him my Syrian passport. This soldier ordered me to stay in the car and he kept my passport with him. He took my passport and went back to the checkpoint to speak to a colleague of his. They talked to each other for about 10 minutes and both of them came back to the car. Then, he asked me to get out of the car and to get my luggage out of the car, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they search your luggage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did they find in your luggage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They found religious books, a copy of the Koran -- an interpretation of the Koran -- and one of the soldiers said to me, "All the stuff that you have got on you is Islamic, you do not have anything Croat on you."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment, I had a cringe, I felt the tension of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did they do to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they finished the search, they handcuffed me and put me in a white Golf -- I think -- at first they took me to the town of Vitez. There, we stopped for five minutes and then continued to the town of Busovaca and, from there, they were given the instructions to take me to Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On the way, were you mistreated in any way from the checkpoint through Vitez and Busovaca, then to Kaonik -- did anyone mistreat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when we were 50 metres away from the Croat checkpoint, torture started -- they started hitting me with their rifle butts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they do this in the car, did they, as you were going along?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, inside the car -- all along the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you got to -- I will just pause there if I may. Your Honour, it may have been attended to, but might we have a redaction -- page 19, lines 19 to 21, and page 20, lines 5 to 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you got to the Kaonik camp, what did these people do then, when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken into a corridor in the camp, and I was asked to go down on my knees. They removed the handcuffs, and they took me to cell number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After they put you into cell number 4, did anything then happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, five or 10 minutes later, four or five individuals, stocky, well-built, ran towards the cell and barged into the cell and they started torturing me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did they do to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They kicked me in the head with their military boots, they started jumping up and down on me. Their kicking centered around the kidneys and the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you lose consciousness at any stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second phase of the torture -- sorry, I should correct myself -- I think it was on the third day -- at one point on the third day I lost consciousness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you cannot recall now whether or not you lost consciousness on this first occasion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, I did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You are unable to remember now whether you lost consciousness on the first occasion, not on the third day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember very well that, on the third day, that is when I lost consciousness -- I had already asked the guard to go to the bathroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not want to take you to the third day, I want to continue on where we are on the first night of your arrival. How long were you beaten for when those four men, those four persons came into the room and started to beat you and kick you -- how long did that last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The torture continued for about 10 minutes on the first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Later on that day, did anything else happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on that very same day, they came back again in the evening and started torturing me again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know who came back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That evening there was Aleksovski and a person -- another person called Dzemo and there was another person called Medugorac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When they came back on this occasion, did any of them speak to you -- did they say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Aleksovski said to me, pointing at Dzemo, "Do you know if this person is Croat or a Muslim?" And I said to him, "It does not make any difference to me."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did he do when you said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said to me, "I can assure you that he is a Muslim and that he works with us."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he say anything to you before that -- before he asked you whether you knew this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the same day, he was cursing at me and he was swearing at Islam.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was he saying, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember one word which I find very difficult to repeat now. It is very insulting to any religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was that, can you say it -- are you able to say it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the sense, if the interpreter understands me, he said, "Fuck your religion."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he do anything to you other than speak to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the second visit in the evening, he started by kicking me hard in the chest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What sort of boots did he have on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The standard military boots.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "he", you are referring to Mr. Aleksovski, are you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, I did not hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "he" kicked you, are you referring to Mr. Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was Aleksovski who kicked me in the chest with his military boots.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Aleksovski at that stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know Mr. Aleksovski before that -- before that encounter on the first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you subsequently come to know him during the period of time you spent in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, other Muslim prisoners told me his name, and told me about him. One of the prisoners, Hamdo Dautovic -- Tovic or Davtovic -- they told me about him, about Mr. Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After Mr. Aleksovski had kicked with his boots, what happened then -- what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Having asked me about Dzemo and explaining to me he was a Muslim but he worked with them, Aleksovski asked Medugorac to give me a cigarette.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he give you the cigarette?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lit the cigarette and had two or three puffs. He asked Medugorac to start kicking me and jump on my back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened, did Medugorac obey this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he followed the instructions. Immediately, as soon as Aleksovski gave him the order, he pounced on me and starting kicking me and jumping over my body.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did Mr. Aleksovski stay in the room while Medugorac was doing this to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how long did this go on for, on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The discussion lasted for about half an hour. But the action, the torture action went on for about four or five minutes. Then, they left the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was the cell door then closed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you later on that day hear a discussion going on in the hallway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard people talking in the corridor and I could hear the English language spoken -- being spoken in the corridors and I heard my name being mentioned. A few days later, I was told by another prisoner that the ICRC were there. But they did not acknowledge my presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you gain the impression that the ICRC were looking for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had that impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "they did not acknowledge your presence", who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am talking about the Croats, the HVO troops, who refused to acknowledge my presence. They said to the ICRC that, "There is no such person by such name."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to why the ICRC would have known you were there -- as to how they would have known that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is something that I found out about later. I found out that the ICRC were always there looking for people, searching for people, and this is something that I only found out about when I was there in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did anything else happen to you on that first day, that you can now remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I will remember later, but at this present moment, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Moving on, after you had stayed there, were you ever questioned or interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: He did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Moving on after the first day, were you ever interrogated when you were at the camp or questioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. On the second day, a number of soldiers came to the camp and I understood that they were sent by Kordic. They started asking me where I came from, why I was in Bosnia, and they asked me about my opinion of the Vance-Owen Plan. At that moment in time, my body was all blackened, marked, and my eyes were black because of the torture that I sustained, and I was in no position to answer any questions and I said to them, "The Vance-Owen Plan has nothing to do with me" and at that moment I broke down and I started to cry. These soldiers did not torture me -- those who interrogated me. I sat in the interrogation room at the beginning of the corridor to the left, and they brought me a coffee and when they realised I could not answer their questions, I was taken back to my cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I notice it is 20 past. Did you wish to have your adjournment at this stage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, I think it might be the right moment. We are now going to have a break until a quarter to 11. (10.23am) (A short break) (10.52am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness, during the period of time that you were in the Kaonik camp, were you ever required to do physical labour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. During my second month of internment, they started to make me work. They gave me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you, but I think that Mr. Mikulicic has something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise for interrupting, but I would like to recall that the incriminating events in the Kaonik camp covered the period from January to the end of May 1993 according to the indictment. The witness said that he was arrested on 25 May, and now he is talking about the second month of his stay in Kaonik, which goes beyond the time frame of the indictment and that is why the Defence objects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, in my submission, the evidence is admissible on a number of grounds. Firstly, your Honours, I submit that it should be admitted, because it is a course of conduct that goes to the narration of the event from the time the witness arrived at this place through to the time that he left. It may be argued that if there was clear evidence that Mr. Aleksovski was not present and no longer was the commander of the camp, clearly on relevance you could say that evidence is not admissible. But if that is not the case, then, in my respectful submission, the event is the period of confinement, the period of being detained, and it starts within the indictment period, and I submit, your Honour, that the narration of that event should go from the time it commences through to the conclusion of that evidence. That is one ground on which I submit it is admissible. Another ground that I submit that it is admissible is that it goes to establish a state of mind. If you have one incident that occurs within the period of this course of conduct at the beginning of the course of conduct and there is no evidence of any further event at all at any stage, one could perhaps mount an argument that the requisite state of mind may not have been established. If subsequent things happen -- they do not have to be in the indictment period, but if subsequent things do happen which can be related back to the event in question, then, in my submission, the evidence is admissible to prove that state of mind. So, it sort of separates it out from being something that can be described as a mere aberration and it goes to prove that there was, through this continuing course of conduct, a state of mind which commenced at one point and concluded at another and all of the events that occurred during that period are, in my submission, your Honour, admissible. It is a bit like, if, for example, an accused participates in a record of interview and says things in a record of interview, which matters are admissible obviously for other reasons, and courts have said they are admissible for entirely different reasons, but one of the reasons why it is admissible is because the court is entitled to look at what the accused says at some subsequent date and some subsequent period of time and to analyse that in order to assist it in determining the state of mind of the accused at the time the offence is committed. This may not be necessarily by way of admission -- it might be false denials or it could be any other number of things that occurred. Another example might be, for example, a situation -- let us assume a hypothetical situation where you have a murder and the indictment relates to that specific event, so it is limited to, say, on or about 15 March 1991 X happened. If the police subsequently find a knife which matches a description and may have found it two years later and that knife can be linked back to the event and linked to the accused, then that is properly admissible -- notwithstanding the fact that it is outside of the indictment period. In my respectful submission, one does not merely say that, because the evidence is outside of the indictment period, that immediately renders it inadmissible. There are bases upon which it is properly admissible. We are dealing here with a situation where we say that the accused is responsible for the commission of certain crimes, and part of the elements which we must prove is: did he intend to do it? Did he have the knowledge, the requisite state of mind to do that? Essentially, it goes to that. Finally, it goes to the question of identification, because, if you have one incident related to you and the witness says, "On this occasion the accused was present," the issue of identification, particularly in a situation where the witness has never met the accused before, is a pregnant issue that needs to be resolved. Evidence of subsequent incidents which happened, particularly of a similar nature, can go to establish identification and to prove, in our respectful submission, that it is indeed the person that the witness says it was on the day -- the initial period. So, your Honours, for all those types of reasons, and particularly because it is a continuing course of conduct, it is my respectful submission that the evidence is properly admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. The Defence fully appreciates the learned opinion of our colleague, the Prosecutor, but we feel that the arguments given by the Prosecutor are not relevant for this particular case. It is a fact that the indictment covers a precise time period, thereby the Defence has been notified of the time period in question and has prepared itself within that framework and is continuing to work within that framework. Any change of the factual contents of the indictment outside this time frame is not acceptable to the Defence, because, de facto, it signifies an amendment of the indictment, referring to events that are not covered by the indictment that has not been issued. I should like to remind your Honours that, in the course of our trial, it has already -- an identical objection has already been made by the Defence. This occurred when a witness started to describe events dating back to July 1993. At the time, the Defence objected. The Prosecution, responding to the Defence's objection, also voiced the opinion that the witness's testimony was necessary for the purpose of identification of the accused. The Defence has no objection to that. It feels that a question of identification can be resolved independently of the events that go beyond the frameworks of the indictment. Therefore, what the Defence does object to is a factual expansion of the charges by questioning the witness on events that are not covered by the indictment. That is the position of the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mikulicic. I think that the Trial Chamber has been sufficiently informed on the matter and we will take a decision, Mr. Niemann, thank you. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, could you repeat the question, please -- the question that you were in the process of asking the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Without looking at the transcript, I cannot remember it precisely, but I will do my best, but the question is: Were you forced to do any labour during the time that you were imprisoned in the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: That forced labour is outside the framework of the indictment, or is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The witness went on to say it was outside of the indictment period, I think, from memory -- some weeks after -- the indictment period ends on 31 May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In that case, the Trial Chamber finds that it is possible to go outside the events within the indictment period, but only to establish the consequences, because we must always have a systematic perspective of the events -- that is the globality -- the events and the consequences thereof, but in this particular case, these are other facts, which are not a consequence of others that are contained in the indictment. That is why the Trial Chamber's decision is that you should withdraw that question, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please. Might I seek a clarification, your Honours? From what you have said, do your Honours wish me to restrict my questioning entirely to the indictment period, or are you saying that any questioning beyond the indictment period must only go to issues such as mens rea and identification. May I seek a clarification of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, it is your first hypothesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please. Witness, Their Honours have made a ruling that you should not tell us about events which occurred beyond 31 May, so it would assist if you can just talk about events that happen within that time frame?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you saying events after 31st?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, only up until 31 May. You do not need to comment -- I just want you to be aware of that. You mentioned on the first occasion you were beaten, when you first arrived. Were you beaten at any time after that, during that time frame?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you tell us about those beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will start from the beginning so I do not lose my train of thought. The first time was on 21 May, I was tortured twice on the same day. The second time was two days later. Then the process of torture was systematic -- it was conducted on a weekly basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, just dealing with the period from 25 May until 31 May, what was the processes of torture that were systematic -- can you describe those for us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, on day one, when I arrived at the prison, I was confronted with four or five men, well-built, and I was subjected to kicking.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about the occasion a couple of days later when you were beaten again, what happened then? Can you describe that beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same method was applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was present on that next beating a couple of days later, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Honestly, I cannot remember the people who were involved, but I know that, on the second round of torture on the first day, Aleksovski was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you were subjected to any psychological mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were threats that I will be handed over to the Chetnik forces, the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who threatened you that you would be handed over to the Chetnik forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the outset it was Aleksovski and all those who work with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why did you think this was psychological mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The beating I thought was a joke -- I thought they were teasing me, but then I came to the conclusion that they were willing to do that, they would hand me over.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But why did you feel that that was psychological mistreatment, are you able to say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How can you describe it otherwise? We all know the Chetnik forces bombed parts of Bosnia and one can imagine the dangers -- both parties were enemies to the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As a result of the beatings that you had, did you suffer any physical injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My body was bloated as a result of the kicking and beating that I received and I was bleeding through the nose and the mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you notice any blood in your urine or anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the first day, it was either on the first day or the third day when I went to the bathroom to urinate and I noticed there was blood coming out of my urine. When I walked out of the bathroom, I fainted and the only thing I can remember was I was being dragged by other inmates back into my cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When were you released from the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 16 August.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how was it that you came to be released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 13 days before my release, Aleksovski came to inform me of that decision. He called me outside the prison, but before they actually physically released me, they tortured me in the camp yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not want you to go into that incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence wanted to object regarding the description of events that occurred outside the indictment period, but if the witness will limit himself to the circumstances of his release, then the Defence has no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage, I wish to argue that anything said to the witness by Mr. Aleksovski at the time of his release is clearly admissible and, if that is to be argued, I would wish to argue that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I think that we should focus on the release and not go any further than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is your Honour preventing me from leading what the accused said to the witness on a subsequent occasion which is relevant to the events? Is that your Honours' ruling?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But the date is beyond the indictment and we have decided that all the facts outside the indictment period, that is, after 31 May, should not be an object of testimony. It is sufficient to know that the witness was released on 16 August.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please. I do not wish to quarrel with your ruling in any way, but I would just like to say that that would mean discussions with a police officer would be inadmissible, because it is not within the indictment period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: No. As you understand, Mr. Niemann, what goes outside the indictment period and which may, in a way, incriminate the accused, cannot be admissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not know that, your Honour. That is not something I am accustomed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: That is the decision of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please. After you left the camp, did you suffer any illnesses or consequences as a result of being in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and to date I suffer from continuous migraine, I cannot concentrate, and, when I am asleep, I cannot breathe properly -- kidney pains -- and this becomes more evident when there is a change of weather.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is there any permanent damage that you know of to any of the organs of your body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Frankly, I have not had an extensive medical check-up. After I left prison, I started suffering from chest pains and heart disorders and I have reached the point where I have given up on trying to find out what is exactly wrong with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The accused, Mr. Aleksovski, do you think that you would recognise him again if you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you point -- could you look around this courtroom and if you can see him; would you point to him for me, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness points to his left in the direction of the accused).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Finally, can you tell us about the conditions that you suffered in the camp -- the hygienic conditions -- were you permitted to shower?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hygiene was non-existent in the camp, because you do not expect to get proper treatment, you do not expect to get hygiene when you are tortured. When you are insulted, when you are tortured physically, how do you expect anybody will give you a shower or give you hygiene?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you given any changes of clothes during the period that you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I did not hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you given any changes of clothes during the period that you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at the outset I was in cell number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think that that has been misinterpreted. Were you given any changes of clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had my luggage with me, and they left me with part of the luggage. I remember they took my brand new pair of shoes and they gave me an old pair. Apart from that, they did not give me anything else. I had my luggage with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Niemann. Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor, if you have questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Mr. T, I am attorney Goran Mikulicic. In this case I represent the Defence and I will now ask you a number of questions, so please be kind enough to answer them to the best of your recollection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. T, could you tell us again what year you reached the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Will you tell me what your intention was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My intention was to study medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When did you enrol at university and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1983, when I completed a course in the Serbo-Croat language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: During your stay in the former Yugoslavia, did you spend any time in other parts of the country except for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was -- for the first three years I was studying in Sarajevo and then from Sarajevo I went to Pristina to continue my studies there and I stayed there for three and a half years and from there I went to Banja Luka and I was there for three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. T, when did you drop out of the university?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I abandoned it when the war began -- I stopped studying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what year that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The end of 1991 -- actually, in the course of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, you studied from 1983 until 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I remember well, you said that you gave up studies on your third year of study?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you did not pass your examinations from your third year of study?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I completed the year of study but not the examinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember which was your last exam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The last exam I took and passed was anatomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what year that subject is in the curriculum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is in the curriculum for the first and second year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. T, during your studies which lasted nine years, how did you finance your studies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My father financed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you employed anywhere at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where were you when the war broke out in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber which ethnic group is predominant in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Members of which ethnic group inhabit Banja Luka in the majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, as far as I know, there was a large number of Muslims in Banja Luka before the war. As far as I know, there were about 48 or 49 per cent of them. I am not sure about those figures, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, when you left Banja Luka the war had already started in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was three months after the war began.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Which military side was in power in Banja Luka at the time? Were they the Croats, the Muslims or the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see, the Serbs. You said that you left Banja Luka in 1992 with a group of students and went to Zagreb; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After that, you said that you decided to help the Bosnian people and that you went back to Bosnia, to Travnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After that, you joined the BiH army and you stayed for seven days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And, after that, you decided to move to Syria?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but not immediately after the seven days. I saw that I was not capable of taking part in the combat operations on the front. I saw that I just could not stand it, so I thought to myself in what other way could I help those people, so I remembered that I could interpret, and I could be a teacher of Arabic for children and for adults sometimes, and after about 10 or 11 months, I decided to leave the country and go to Syria.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what was it that motivated you to decide to go to Syria?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My desire to see my relatives in Syria.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was it not simpler to go to Syria from Zagreb when you were in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I told you that I wanted to stand with the Bosnian people, to help them as much as I could, so I thought to myself I will take part up to such a point and then I will go back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. T, during the time you were in Travnik, you told us that you spent a short time in the BiH Army, after which you taught Arabic as well as Arabic culture and religion. Where did you get the finances for this? Did you charge for these services or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was doing that, there were quite a number of humanitarian organisations which encouraged me -- when they saw me holding these courses, they would give me some kind of a gift, compensation, for what I was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I understood you well, you said that humanitarian organisations gave you money to teach Arabic culture and language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No -- to teach Arabic language as a teacher of children of religion -- to teach the children the basics of Islam.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Then you decided to see your family and go to Syria. What were the things you took with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took all my suitcases with me, what ever I had in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how many suitcases were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were four of them, or five -- I cannot remember exactly, but four or five.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that you had some religious books with you, some holy books?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Apart from these holy books, did you have any other literature on you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. T, that apart from holy books, you also had some literature on how to lead a jihad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had nothing about leading a jihad, no literature of that kind, but I had Islamic religious books.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let me try and ask you a different question. In the books that you had, was "jihad" mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it might be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Trial Chamber what is "jihad"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Jihad" is the holy war or the combat on the path of God.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who is this holy war against?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mainly against evil.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What kind of evil -- I do not understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Against injustice, against evil.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. T, you said that you had been stopped on 25 May in a vehicle, but you were not in the convoy but in front of the convoy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Witness T, what motivated you to drive in front of the convoy and not within the convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was my mistake to listen to the other people, so I obeyed other people's advice and that is why that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does it mean that you had nothing to do with the United Nations convoy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I wanted to go with those lorries, because the situation was very tense at that time -- the situation between the BiH army and the HVO, and I kind of thought the best thing would be to go with the lorries in the convoy, but things were different -- somebody told me, "Why do you not go in this car" and that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Witness T, can you recall how the soldiers that arrested you on 25 May were dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO soldiers were wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you go back to that time period? Can you make a difference between the military police and the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean their army?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I do not know what "their" is, I mean the HVO army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot exactly, I cannot differentiate, because I did not pay any attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that military police wear white belts on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did those soldiers wear white belts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that you were handcuffed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where did these handcuffs come from -- do you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How can I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Witness T, you said that, when you were stopped at the checkpoint, you handed over your passport?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Before that, you said that you arrived on the territory of the former Yugoslavia in 1982. During your stay in the former Yugoslavia, did you register yourself with the police authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you get any identification papers from the police authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nothing in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I object on two bases. One on relevance -- I cannot see the relevance of this question at all and secondly again on the principle that it is outside the indictment period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I will seize this opportunity to ask the witness: what passport have you got on you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I was just changing my earphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: My question was: what passport does the witness have on him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My Syrian passport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I think that you have to take into account the dates. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will ask my question in a different way, so I can respect the time frame. On 25 May 1993, did you have any other kind of identification on you apart from the Syrian passport?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Before that day, or on that day -- in the time when you were arrested in Banja Luka, did you have any other identification given to you, apart from the Syrian passport?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you have a residence permit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is that not an identification card?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The residence permit is actually a stamp that is put on your passport. It is not a separate identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. From that checkpoint on, you said that for a short time you stopped at Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was Vitez we stopped for five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And after that you came --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were probably given the order to continue towards Busovaca and Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that, in fact, during that journey you did not stop anywhere for any length of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the soldiers that were with you in the car beat you during the journey?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With rifle butts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did they injure you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no blood, but I received a few blows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you have any pain from that -- did you suffer any pain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how -- you mean whether I felt any pain?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you feel any pain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were very hard blows in the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you suffer any pain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was normal I felt pain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did anyone, upon your arrival at Kaonik, register you? Did any of the officials in the prison of Kaonik register you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But the first day when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Around what time did you arrive at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the afternoon -- it might have been 3, 3.30 -- it could have been between 2.30 and 3.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Nobody registered you then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When did the Red Cross register you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the third or fourth day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On your first day at Kaonik, were you approached by one of the guards -- one of the guards of the prison at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to any of the guards in the Kaonik prison on the first day that you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked them not to hit me -- that is what I told the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
